questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with Crohn's disease has needed courses of oral prednisolone 40 mg for most of the past 9 months. She has gained 9 kg around her abdomen, has a round red face and bruises easily. Her BP is 148/90 mmHg. Her 9am plasma ACTH is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her presentation?
questions.e: Exogenous steroid is the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome overall, and negative feedback suppresses ACTH. Always exclude it first.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: oral prednisolone 40 mg for most of the past 9 months
steps.x: Cushingoid features after months of high-dose prednisolone, with ACTH suppressed by negative feedback.

elim: Also gives low ACTH, but the commonest cause overall is the steroid she is already taking.
ACTH-dependent: ACTH would be normal or high, not low.
ACTH would be very high, usually with weight loss and pigmentation.
Causes weight gain and hirsutism, but not bruising and suppressed ACTH.

steps.x: **D. Exogenous corticosteroid use.** Cushingoid on steroids = exogenous cause; check the drug history first.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a 2 year history of weight gain, thin skin and hypertension. She takes no medication. Her overnight dexamethasone suppression test and 24-hour urinary free cortisol are both abnormal. Her 9am plasma ACTH is undetectable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Confirmed cortisol excess with suppressed ACTH and no steroid use is ACTH-independent; a solitary adrenal adenoma is the commonest endogenous cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Two abnormal screens confirm Cushing's; undetectable ACTH makes it ACTH-independent.

elim: Pituitary ACTH secretion: ACTH is normal or raised.
ACTH-dependent with very high ACTH.
Low ACTH fits, but she takes no medication.
Needs chronic alcohol excess and has no true HPA axis abnormality.

steps.x: **A. Adrenal adenoma.** Low ACTH, no steroids = adrenal cause; adenoma is the commonest endogenous cause.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has confirmed Cushing's syndrome with purple striae and proximal weakness. She takes no medication. Her 9am plasma ACTH is 88 ng/L (7–63). On a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, both her cortisol and ACTH fall by more than half.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: High ACTH makes it ACTH-dependent, and suppression of both cortisol and ACTH on high-dose dexamethasone points to a pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: both her cortisol and ACTH fall by more than half
steps.x: ACTH-dependent and suppressible on high dose: pituitary.

elim: ACTH-independent: ACTH would be suppressed.
ACTH-independent with low ACTH.
Neither cortisol nor ACTH suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone.
She takes no medication, and ACTH would be low.

steps.x: **C. Cushing's disease.** High ACTH + suppresses on high dose = Cushing's disease.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has gained weight over 18 months and has developed a round face and a fat pad over his upper back. His BP is 158/96 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm. His capillary glucose is 13.1 mmol/L. He has noticed difficulty getting up from low chairs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his legs?
o: Absent ankle reflexes with stocking sensory loss
Weakness of hip flexion with thigh wasting
questions.e: Cortisol excess causes protein catabolism, giving proximal muscle weakness and wasting: difficulty standing from sitting.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: round face and a fat pad over his upper back
difficulty getting up from low chairs
steps.x: Moon face and buffalo hump with trouble rising from a chair: proximal myopathy.

elim: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, distal and sensory, not his complaint.
Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy in young males.
Common peroneal palsy or neuropathy: distal, not proximal.
A lower motor neurone sign of motor neurone disease.

steps.x: **E. Weakness of hip flexion with thigh wasting.** Cushing's myopathy is proximal: test standing from sitting.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has gained weight around her abdomen over a year despite dieting. She bruises after minor knocks and a cut on her shin has not healed after 6 weeks. Her BP is 154/94 mmHg. She takes no regular medication.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her abdomen?
o: Pale silvery striae under 5 mm wide
questions.e: Wide purple (violaceous) striae are the classic skin sign of cortisol excess, from protein catabolism thinning the dermis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Central obesity, easy bruising and poor wound healing: thin skin from catabolic cortisol.

elim: Portal hypertension in chronic liver disease.
Flank bruising in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Old, healed stretch marks (e.g. pregnancy), not the classic Cushing's striae.
Excess oestrogen in liver disease or pregnancy.

steps.x: **E. Wide purple striae.** Cushing's striae are wide and purple.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman is referred by her GP with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Over a year she has developed a round plethoric face, a dorsocervical fat pad and thin arms and legs with a large abdomen. Her BP is 162/100 mmHg. She takes no steroids.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Moon face, buffalo hump and central obesity with thin limbs plus new diabetes and hypertension are the picture of cortisol excess.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: thin arms and legs with a large abdomen
steps.x: Central fat redistribution with thin limbs is the discriminating feature over simple obesity.

elim: Weight gain and fatigue, but not moon face, buffalo hump and new diabetes.
Central obesity, diabetes and hypertension, but no moon face, buffalo hump or thin limbs.
Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with weight loss.
Weight gain and hirsutism, but not this fat redistribution.

steps.x: **A. Cushing's syndrome.** Moon face + buffalo hump + thin limbs = Cushing's syndrome.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes has lost 6 kg in 6 weeks and has severe leg weakness and ankle swelling. His BP is 176/104 mmHg. His plasma ACTH is markedly raised and his 8am cortisol does not suppress after dexamethasone. A venous blood gas is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood gas?
questions.e: Very high cortisol (especially from ectopic ACTH) acts on mineralocorticoid receptors, giving the characteristic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A rapid ectopic ACTH picture in a smoker: cortisol levels high enough to act like aldosterone.

elim: Adrenal insufficiency or renal failure: the opposite pattern.
Diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis.
DKA, lactate or toxins.
Hyperventilation; does not explain the cortisol-driven picture.

steps.x: **B. Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.** Cushing's (ectopic especially) = low K, high bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has a 4 month history of rapidly developing acne, a deepening voice, facial hair and purple striae. Her BP is 168/98 mmHg. Her plasma ACTH is suppressed and serum androgens are markedly raised. CT shows an irregular 9 cm left adrenal mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: An ACTH-independent cause with rapid onset, virilisation and a large irregular adrenal mass suggests the rare adrenal carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: rapidly developing acne, a deepening voice
steps.x: Suppressed ACTH = adrenal source; size, irregularity and androgen co-secretion = malignant.

elim: Commonest adrenal cause, but usually small, smooth and cortisol-only.
Rare familial condition with cardiac myxomas and spotty skin pigmentation.
ACTH-dependent: ACTH would not be suppressed.
ACTH would be very high.

steps.x: **B. Adrenal carcinoma.** Large irregular adrenal mass + virilisation = adrenal carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has fatigue, low mood, central weight gain and easy bruising. Her BP is 150/94 mmHg. She takes no medication and drinks little alcohol. Her GP suspects Cushing's syndrome and asks for a test that reflects loss of the normal daily cortisol rhythm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: High 9am cortisol with normal midnight cortisol
Low 9am cortisol on a short Synacthen test
questions.e: Cortisol normally falls to its lowest at midnight; in Cushing's this diurnal variation is lost, so late-night salivary cortisol is raised.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: fatigue, low mood, central weight gain
loss of the normal daily cortisol rhythm
steps.x: Cushing's flattens the diurnal curve: the midnight trough is lost.

elim: This is the normal pattern, with a preserved rhythm.
Adrenal insufficiency, the opposite condition.
Normal; a low midnight value argues against Cushing's.
Cortisol excess raises urinary free cortisol.

steps.x: **D. Raised late-night salivary cortisol.** Lost diurnal rhythm = high late-night cortisol.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with sarcoidosis has taken prednisolone 30 mg daily for 2 years and is Cushingoid. He stopped it a week ago because of weight gain. He now has vomiting, abdominal pain and dizziness. His BP is 78/44 mmHg and pulse rate 118 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Long-term steroids suppress the HPA axis, so stopping abruptly leaves the adrenals unable to make cortisol: adrenal crisis with shock and hyponatraemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Abrupt cessation after long-term steroids, then vomiting and shock.

elim: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with high amylase; no link to stopping steroids.
Needs hyperglycaemia and ketones; low sodium and high potassium point to cortisol lack.
Sarcoidosis is not an infection, and there is no source.
Gives peritonism and free air, and steroids were stopped, not continued.

steps.x: **B. Adrenal crisis.** Long-term steroids stopped suddenly = adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has hypertension, ankle oedema and hypokalaemia. His plasma ACTH is 240 ng/L (7–63). On a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test neither his cortisol nor ACTH falls. Pituitary MRI is normal. CT chest shows a 2 cm well-defined central lung lesion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: No suppression of cortisol or ACTH on high-dose dexamethasone means an ectopic ACTH source; in a young non-smoker a carcinoid is more likely than small cell cancer.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: neither his cortisol nor ACTH falls
steps.x: Very high ACTH, no suppression and a lung lesion: ectopic ACTH.

elim: ACTH would be suppressed.
Would suppress on high dose and show a pituitary adenoma.
ACTH would be low.
Needs alcohol excess; ACTH would not be this high.

steps.x: **B. Bronchial carcinoid tumour secreting ACTH.** Ectopic ACTH = no suppression on high dose; small cell lung cancer and carcinoid are the usual sources.

questions.stem: A 52 year old publican drinks about 80 units of alcohol a week. He has a round red face, central obesity and hypertension. His overnight dexamethasone suppression test and late-night salivary cortisol are both abnormal. His liver enzymes are raised.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Repeat testing after 1 month of alcohol abstinence
questions.e: Chronic alcohol excess causes pseudo-Cushing's: the clinical and biochemical picture without true HPA axis disease. Repeat testing after a month of abstinence.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Heavy drinking can make the screening tests falsely abnormal.

elim: Imaging comes only after true Cushing's is confirmed and ACTH is low.
Localises a confirmed cause; first exclude pseudo-Cushing's.
A specialist localisation test for confirmed ACTH-dependent disease.
Only for confirmed ACTH-dependent disease.

steps.x: **E. Repeat testing after 1 month of alcohol abstinence.** Alcohol + abnormal cortisol tests = think pseudo-Cushing's; abstain for a month, then retest.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has central obesity, purple striae and proximal weakness. Her overnight dexamethasone test and 24-hour urinary free cortisol both confirm cortisol excess. The endocrinologist explains how the diagnosis will be fully confirmed and the cause found.
questions.q: Which combination of investigations is the gold standard for this?
o: Dexamethasone suppression testing, plasma ACTH and imaging
Short Synacthen test and adrenal CT
Thyroid function tests and pituitary MRI
questions.e: The overall gold standard is dexamethasone suppression testing plus plasma ACTH plus imaging: confirm, classify as ACTH-dependent or not, then image the right gland.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: fully confirmed and the cause found
steps.x: Confirming and finding the cause needs three things: suppression testing, ACTH and imaging.

elim: Random cortisol is unhelpful (diurnal variation); imaging before ACTH may find incidentalomas.
Low potassium is a feature, not a diagnostic test.
Synacthen tests for adrenal insufficiency.
Thyroid tests do not assess cortisol.

steps.x: **A. Dexamethasone suppression testing, plasma ACTH and imaging.** Suppression test + ACTH + imaging, in that order.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man with epilepsy controlled on carbamazepine has gained weight, developed purple abdominal striae and has a BP of 152/96 mmHg. He takes no steroids. His GP wants to screen for Cushing's syndrome.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Carbamazepine induces CYP450 and speeds dexamethasone metabolism, causing false positive suppression tests; use 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol instead.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
A CYP450 inducer makes the dexamethasone test unreliable.

elim: Imaging before biochemical confirmation is wrong.
A localising test after confirmation, and also affected by carbamazepine.
Usually first-line but contraindicated with CYP450 inducers like carbamazepine.
Varies through the day and is not a screening test.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour urinary free cortisol.** Phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin: avoid the dexamethasone test; use urinary or salivary cortisol.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with suspected Cushing's syndrome is given 1 mg dexamethasone orally at 11pm. Her plasma cortisol is measured at 8am the next morning. She takes no other medication.
questions.q: Which result is most consistent with Cushing's syndrome?
questions.e: Normally 1 mg dexamethasone suppresses morning cortisol (below about 50 nmol/L); in Cushing's syndrome cortisol is not suppressed.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
The overnight low-dose test: dexamethasone at 11pm, cortisol at 8am.

elim: ACTH is measured later to classify the cause, not as the screening result.
Normal suppression: argues against Cushing's.
Hyperglycaemia is a feature, not the test result.
A feature, not part of this test.

steps.x: **C. 8am cortisol not suppressed (above 50 nmol/L).** Cushing's = failure to suppress cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with obesity and hypertension had an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, with an 8am cortisol of 96 nmol/L. She takes no medication and does not drink alcohol. Her GP refers her to endocrinology.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Two abnormal screening tests are usually needed to confirm Cushing's syndrome, so a second screen (24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol) comes next.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
One abnormal screen is not enough to confirm the diagnosis.

elim: Imaging only after confirmation and an ACTH level.
Looks for an ectopic source, far too early.
Localises after the diagnosis is confirmed.
Only for confirmed ACTH-dependent disease.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour urinary free cortisol.** Confirm with two abnormal screens before localising.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has confirmed Cushing's syndrome. Her plasma ACTH is 79 ng/L (7–63). On high-dose dexamethasone, her cortisol and ACTH both fall by over 50%. She takes no medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: High ACTH that suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone is Cushing's disease, so image the pituitary with MRI.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
ACTH-dependent and suppressible: look at the pituitary.

elim: For ACTH-independent disease with low ACTH.
Hunts for an ectopic source, which would not suppress.
Localises neuroendocrine (ectopic) tumours.
Irrelevant to cortisol excess.

steps.x: **D. Pituitary MRI.** ACTH-dependent = pituitary MRI; ACTH-independent = adrenal CT.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has confirmed Cushing's syndrome. Adrenal CT shows a smooth 3 cm right adrenal nodule. She takes no steroids. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is performed to support the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result?
o: Cortisol and ACTH both not suppressed, ACTH high
Cortisol and ACTH both suppressed, ACTH high
questions.e: An adrenal adenoma secretes cortisol autonomously, so cortisol does not suppress, while ACTH is already suppressed by negative feedback.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Autonomous adrenal cortisol: no suppression, ACTH switched off.

elim: Ectopic ACTH secretion.
Cushing's disease (pituitary).
Not a recognised pattern for an adrenal tumour.
Suppression would argue against autonomous adrenal secretion.

steps.x: **C. Cortisol not suppressed, ACTH low.** Pituitary: both suppress. Adrenal: cortisol doesn't, ACTH low. Ectopic: neither.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with asthma has taken prednisolone 10 mg daily for 18 months. She has a moon face, thin skin and proximal weakness. Her asthma is now well controlled on inhaled therapy. She asks whether she can stop the prednisolone today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Switch to an equivalent dose of dexamethasone
questions.e: Exogenous Cushing's is treated by weaning the steroid gradually; stopping abruptly risks adrenal crisis because the HPA axis is suppressed.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Iatrogenic Cushing's and the indication has gone.

elim: She no longer needs it, and it is causing harm.
Blocks endogenous cortisol synthesis; useless for exogenous steroids.
Abrupt cessation after long-term use risks adrenal crisis.
Still glucocorticoid excess.

steps.x: **B. Gradually reduce the prednisolone.** Exogenous Cushing's: wean slowly, never stop abruptly.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has confirmed ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome. Her plasma ACTH is suppressed and adrenal CT shows a 3.5 cm smooth, low-attenuation left adrenal adenoma. The right adrenal looks normal. Her BP is controlled on amlodipine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma is treated by removing the affected adrenal (usually laparoscopically).

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: 3.5 cm smooth, low-attenuation left adrenal adenoma
steps.x: A single benign adrenal source.

elim: Unnecessary with a normal right adrenal, and risks lifelong insufficiency and Nelson's.
For an ectopic malignant source.
Controls cortisol before surgery, not definitive treatment.
For a pituitary (ACTH-dependent) cause.

steps.x: **C. Left adrenalectomy.** Adrenal tumour = adrenalectomy.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man who smokes has small cell lung cancer. He has developed rapid weight gain in his face, ankle oedema, potassium of 2.6 mmol/L and a very high plasma ACTH that does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. He is fit for treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management of his cortisol excess?
questions.e: Ectopic ACTH secretion is treated by treating the underlying malignancy; metyrapone can control cortisol meanwhile.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone
steps.x: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer.

elim: A last resort only if the source cannot be treated.
Adds more glucocorticoid.
Helps the potassium but does not treat the cause.
For a pituitary adenoma; the source here is the lung.

steps.x: **E. Treat the underlying lung cancer.** Ectopic ACTH: treat the tumour.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a confirmed cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma and is listed for adrenalectomy in 6 weeks. Her BP is 178/108 mmHg despite two drugs, her HbA1c is 82 mmol/mol and she has a leg ulcer that will not heal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment while she waits for surgery?
questions.e: Metyrapone, a steroid synthesis inhibitor, lowers cortisol before definitive surgery, improving blood pressure, glucose and wound healing.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Severe cortisol effects while awaiting surgery: lower cortisol medically.

elim: A glucocorticoid: worsens cortisol excess.
A mineralocorticoid replacement for adrenal insufficiency.
Replacement, given after surgery, not before.
For acromegaly or neuroendocrine tumours.

steps.x: **D. Metyrapone.** Cortisol control before surgery = metyrapone.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man is reviewed a year after successful transsphenoidal surgery for Cushing's disease. He still has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. A DEXA scan shows a T-score of −2.8 at the lumbar spine. His renal function and calcium are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
questions.e: Long-term management treats the complications: hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis. Bisphosphonates are first-line for osteoporosis.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: renal function and calcium are normal
steps.x: Osteoporosis from previous glucocorticoid excess.

elim: Not used for long-term osteoporosis in the UK.
More glucocorticoid worsens bone loss.
Surgery was successful; the problem is a complication.
Reserved for severe or bisphosphonate-failed cases.

steps.x: **A. Alendronic acid.** After cure, keep treating BP, diabetes and bones.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had bilateral adrenalectomy 4 years ago for Cushing's disease. She takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She now has headaches, darkening skin and a bitemporal hemianopia. Her plasma ACTH is very high and MRI shows an enlarging pituitary adenoma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: This is Nelson's syndrome: loss of cortisol feedback after bilateral adrenalectomy lets the pituitary adenoma grow. It is managed with transsphenoidal surgery.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
An enlarging adenoma with pigmentation and a field defect after bilateral adrenalectomy.

elim: Does not treat a tumour threatening her vision.
She has no adrenals to block.
Unsafe with an established visual field defect.
She has no adrenals and needs mineralocorticoid replacement.

steps.x: **E. Transsphenoidal surgery.** Nelson's syndrome = transsphenoidal surgery.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with Cushing's disease shows a medical student the wide purple striae on her abdomen and the bruises on her forearms. She also says her skin tears easily and cuts take weeks to heal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these skin changes?
o: Catabolic breakdown of dermal protein and collagen
questions.e: Prolonged glucocorticoid excess is catabolic to protein, thinning skin and connective tissue: striae, bruising, tearing and poor wound healing.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Thin, fragile skin that heals poorly.

elim: Androgens cause acne and hirsutism, and would not thin skin.
Causes oedema and hypertension, not fragile skin.
Bruising here is from fragile vessels and thin skin, not platelets.
Scurvy causes perifollicular haemorrhage and gum disease.

steps.x: **B. Catabolic breakdown of dermal protein and collagen.** Cortisol is catabolic to protein: thin skin, striae, bruising.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with Cushing's syndrome from an adrenal adenoma has a fasting glucose of 9.4 mmol/L and an HbA1c of 61 mmol/mol. He has no family history of diabetes and his BMI was normal two years ago.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hyperglycaemia?
questions.e: Cortisol excess causes insulin resistance and increased gluconeogenesis, so diabetes is a metabolic effect of Cushing's.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
New diabetes from an endocrine cause: cortisol is an insulin counter-regulatory hormone.

elim: Type 1 diabetes, with ketosis in younger patients.
Glucagonoma, with a necrolytic migratory rash.
Haemochromatosis.
Chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea.

steps.x: **C. Glucocorticoid-induced insulin resistance.** Cortisol = insulin resistance, central fat and hypertension.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with ectopic ACTH secretion from a carcinoid tumour has a potassium of 2.5 mmol/L and bicarbonate of 36 mmol/L. Her plasma renin and aldosterone are both low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her electrolyte abnormality?
o: Aldosterone excess from an adrenal adenoma
Intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity of very high cortisol
questions.e: At very high concentrations (typically ectopic ACTH) cortisol acts on renal mineralocorticoid receptors, causing hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with low renin and aldosterone.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: renin and aldosterone are both low
steps.x: Hypokalaemic alkalosis but aldosterone and renin are suppressed: something else is acting on the receptor.

elim: Conn's would have high aldosterone.
No vomiting or diarrhoea, and it would not explain her source.
No diuretic history; renin would be high.
Renin is low.

steps.x: **C. Intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity of very high cortisol.** Very high cortisol overwhelms the kidney and behaves like aldosterone.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with untreated Cushing's syndrome for several years falls from standing and sustains a vertebral compression fracture. She is premenopausal and has no other risk factors. DEXA shows reduced bone density.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her bone loss?
o: Suppressed osteoblast activity with increased bone resorption
Vitamin D deficiency with defective mineralisation
questions.e: Chronic glucocorticoid excess suppresses bone formation by osteoblasts and increases resorption, causing osteoporosis and fragility fractures.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: untreated Cushing's syndrome for several years
steps.x: A fragility fracture in a premenopausal woman with long-standing cortisol excess.

elim: Primary hyperparathyroidism; no hypercalcaemia mentioned.
The opposite: cortisol suppresses osteoblasts.
Osteomalacia with bone pain and low phosphate.
Myeloma or metastases.

steps.x: **C. Suppressed osteoblast activity with increased bone resorption.** Cortisol suppresses osteoblasts: osteoporosis.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with Cushing's disease awaiting surgery has had three chest infections and oral candidiasis in 4 months. He has no diabetes, his HIV test is negative and his full blood count is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his recurrent infections?
questions.e: Chronic glucocorticoid excess impairs immune function, increasing the risk of bacterial and fungal infection.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: three chest infections and oral candidiasis
steps.x: Recurrent bacterial and fungal infection with cortisol excess and no other cause.

elim: Typically recurrent Neisseria infections from childhood.
No proteinuria or oedema described.
His blood count is normal.
Encapsulated organism sepsis after splenectomy.

steps.x: **B. Glucocorticoid-induced impairment of immune function.** Cortisol excess = immunosuppression = infections.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. On high-dose dexamethasone his cortisol and ACTH stay unchanged. A small cell lung cancer is later found. His registrar asks why the test result differs from Cushing's disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Dexamethasone is not absorbed in lung cancer
Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumours do not respond to glucocorticoid negative feedback
The pituitary is hypersensitive to dexamethasone
questions.e: A pituitary corticotroph adenoma keeps partial negative feedback and suppresses at high dose; ectopic sources usually show no suppression at either dose.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Ectopic ACTH ignores feedback.

elim: There is no such absorption defect.
Would not explain unchanged ACTH.
ACTH-independent disease would have low ACTH.
A hypersensitive pituitary would suppress.

steps.x: **B. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumours do not respond to glucocorticoid negative feedback.** Pituitary keeps partial feedback; ectopic tumours have none.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with lupus has taken high-dose prednisolone for a year and is Cushingoid. Her 9am plasma ACTH is undetectable and both adrenal glands appear small on an abdominal CT done for another reason.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her ACTH result?
o: Negative feedback of prednisolone on the pituitary
questions.e: Exogenous steroids suppress CRH and ACTH by negative feedback; without ACTH the adrenals atrophy.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Exogenous glucocorticoid switches off the HPA axis.

elim: Would show a large adrenal mass, not small adrenals.
A rare cause of hypopituitarism, not Cushingoid features.
ACTH would be very high.
Sudden headache and visual loss.

steps.x: **D. Negative feedback of prednisolone on the pituitary.** Exogenous steroids = low ACTH by negative feedback.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man had central obesity, a plethoric face and an abnormal overnight dexamethasone suppression test while drinking 70 units of alcohol a week. He completed alcohol detox and has been abstinent for 6 weeks. Repeat dexamethasone testing and urinary free cortisol are now normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his original results?
o: Cyclical Cushing's from an ectopic source
questions.e: Chronic alcohol excess gives Cushingoid signs and abnormal biochemistry without true HPA axis disease; results normalise after a month of abstinence.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Abnormal tests that normalise with abstinence.

elim: Autonomous secretion would not resolve with abstinence.
A pituitary adenoma would not switch off with abstinence.
Rare, and the alcohol link explains the pattern.
No steroid history given.

steps.x: **E. Pseudo-Cushing's syndrome.** Alcohol + Cushingoid + normal after 1 month dry = pseudo-Cushing's.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman had bilateral adrenalectomy 5 years ago after failed pituitary surgery for Cushing's disease. She now has frontal headaches and her skin has darkened markedly. Her plasma ACTH is 1450 ng/L (7–63) and MRI shows a pituitary macroadenoma touching the optic chiasm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her visual fields?
questions.e: Nelson's syndrome: after bilateral adrenalectomy the adenoma enlarges and compresses the optic chiasm, typically causing a bitemporal hemianopia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Nelson's syndrome with a macroadenoma at the chiasm.

elim: Optic neuritis or a lesion of one optic nerve.
Lesion behind the chiasm, e.g. stroke in the optic tract or radiation.
Right parietal lobe lesion.
Glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa.

steps.x: **A. Bitemporal hemianopia.** Chiasm compression = bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man who smokes has a 3 month history of weakness, weight loss and ankle oedema. His BP is 170/100 mmHg. His potassium is 2.7 mmol/L and his plasma ACTH is 310 ng/L (7–63).
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Very high ACTH, as in ectopic ACTH secretion, causes increased skin pigmentation alongside the other features of cortisol excess.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Ectopic ACTH in a smoker: ACTH so high it darkens the skin.

elim: Thyroid enlargement is not part of cortisol excess.
Copper in Wilson's disease.
Graves' disease.
Loss of pigment, linked with autoimmune Addison's.

steps.x: **A. Generalised skin hyperpigmentation.** High ACTH = pigmentation; low ACTH (adrenal or exogenous) = no pigmentation.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman is referred to psychiatry with a year of low mood, poor sleep and irritability. The psychiatrist notices a round face, supraclavicular fat pads, purple abdominal striae and bruised forearms. Her BP is 156/98 mmHg. She takes no medication.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Mood changes are common in cortisol excess; with moon face, striae, bruising and hypertension the unifying diagnosis is Cushing's syndrome.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: low mood, poor sleep and irritability
purple abdominal striae and bruised forearms
steps.x: Psychiatric symptoms plus physical signs of cortisol excess.

elim: Does not explain striae, bruising and hypertension.
Low mood and weight gain but no striae or bruising.
Primary depression would not cause these physical signs.
There are objective physical signs.

steps.x: **B. Cushing's syndrome.** Mood change with purple striae and bruising: test for Cushing's.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has confirmed Cushing's syndrome with a plasma ACTH of 205 ng/L (7–63). On high-dose dexamethasone neither cortisol nor ACTH suppresses. Pituitary MRI is normal. She is an ex-smoker with a 3 month history of cough.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: No suppression on high-dose dexamethasone with high ACTH means an ectopic source, so image the chest (small cell or carcinoid) and abdomen.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Ectopic ACTH pattern: find the tumour.

elim: Used in primary aldosteronism lateralisation.
The diagnosis is already confirmed.
For adrenal insufficiency.
Not a source of ACTH here.

steps.x: **B. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.** Neither suppresses = ectopic: CT chest first.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 2 years and is Cushingoid. He develops a fever of 38.6°C with a cough and is treated at home with antibiotics. He is eating and drinking. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about his prednisolone?
o: Double the prednisolone dose while unwell
questions.e: His HPA axis is suppressed by long-term steroids, so during febrile illness he needs extra glucocorticoid (sick day rules) to avoid adrenal crisis.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Long-term steroid user, intercurrent febrile illness, but able to take tablets.

elim: Reduces cortisol when demand is higher: risks crisis.
Abrupt cessation risks adrenal crisis.
Inhaled steroid does not replace systemic needs.
His suppressed adrenals cannot mount a stress response.

steps.x: **A. Double the prednisolone dose while unwell.** Sick day rules: double the dose; never stop suddenly.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has persistent Cushing's disease after two transsphenoidal operations. Her team plans bilateral adrenalectomy to control her cortisol. She asks what follow-up she will need to detect the main late complication of this operation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term monitoring?
questions.e: Bilateral adrenalectomy removes cortisol feedback, so the adenoma can enlarge (Nelson's syndrome). Monitor with ACTH and pituitary MRI; treat with transsphenoidal surgery.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
The late complication of bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease is Nelson's syndrome.

elim: The adrenals will have been removed.
Looks for an ectopic source, not relevant.
Not linked to Nelson's syndrome.
Parathyroid disease is not the complication.

steps.x: **D. Plasma ACTH and pituitary MRI.** After bilateral adrenalectomy, watch the pituitary for Nelson's.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has Nelson's syndrome after bilateral adrenalectomy. His skin is dark, especially in his palmar creases and an old scar. His plasma ACTH is extremely high.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pigmentation?
o: ACTH acting on melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes
questions.e: ACTH (and related POMC peptides) stimulate melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes, so very high ACTH darkens the skin.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Pigmentation tracks ACTH, not cortisol: he has no adrenals yet is dark.

elim: He has no adrenals and no endogenous cortisol.
Seen in venous stasis on the lower legs.
Haemochromatosis gives bronze skin but ACTH would not be high.
Causes melasma, not crease pigmentation.

steps.x: **A. ACTH acting on melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes.** Pigmentation = high ACTH via melanocortin-1 receptors.
